transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (AtlasIQ Lead ML), Tom Willis (AtlasIQ Infra), Sara Kline (AtlasIQ CTO)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be imperfect):
We walked through runtime overheads for structured JSON outputs and function/tool calling; SE did a profiling pass showing where tokens and constrained decoding add CPU/GPU work, discussed KV cache hit patterns, batching tradeoffs, and quantization knobs. Customer expressed concerns about on-prem VPC latency and opaque inference costs. Action items: run microbenchmarks, share private-deploy checklist, provide sample result CSVs and configs.

Topics: runtime profiling, function call path latency, JSON strictness overhead, constrained decode costs, KV cache latency, batching strategies, quantization effects, VPC/on-prem networking impact, next steps for pilot.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: okay everyone, thanks for joining, we know this is a deep dive so we'll focus on the runtime numbers and practical mitigation approaches. Arjun will drive the profiling section.
[00:18] Arjun: cool hi all, I'll share my screen after a sec. Quick agenda: measure: function-call + json-mode overhead, measure: token-level GPU time, KV hit/miss microbench, batching sweep, and implications for a VPC/on-prem setup.
[00:35] Priya: great, we're most worried about calls that need strict JSON schema output; our relayer expects deterministic json, and we saw p99 spikes in prod.
[00:45] Tom: and from infra side latency out of our VPC to hosted endpoints varies, so we're exploring private or dedicated.
[01:00] Arjun: understood. First slide: baseline decode without constraints versus with 'json-strict' constrained decoding. Important note: constrained decode adds token-level rejection and resampling logic which increases per-token work on the runtime and sometimes forces extra logits computations.
[01:26] Arjun: in our microbench -- this is on an A100-style node -- unconstrained decode generates at ~90 tokens/s out-of-the-box; when we enable strict structure enforcement (json-mode) we saw 20-40% throughput reduction, p50 impact smaller, p95/p99 much larger.
[01:52] Priya: hmm 20-40% is larger than expected, is that mostly CPU overhead or GPU?
[02:00] Arjun: mixed. There's a GPU kernel overhead from repeated top-k/top-p recalculations when you force constraints, plus CPU-side token validation and possible re-tokenization for partial outputs. Also, if you use a function-calling shim that serializes and validates JSON on the host side, that can add 5-40ms depending on schema complexity.
[02:28] Tom: does Redwood do validation in the runtime or in the SDK? we try to minimize host round trips.
[02:35] Maya: short answer: depends. For hosted we provide the constrained decoding in-run as an option; the SDK-level validation is opt-in and can be moved to runtime for lower latency but more GPU cycles.
[02:50] Sara: is there an easy knob to trade off the GPU compute vs extra CPU validation?
[02:56] Arjun: yes -- quantization and caching. If you accept slightly lower float fidelity (int8/4-bit quant profiles) you free up cycles and can tolerate extra constrained-decoding overhead; conversely you can enable prefix/KV cache to avoid repeated compute for common prefixes so the incremental cost of constrained steps is amortized.
[03:20] Arjun: quick KV cache demo data: with a 70% KV hit rate for conversational reuse we reduced per-call GPU time by ~35%. But the important piece is hit distribution: if hits cluster at early sequences you get better latency SLOs.
[03:42] Priya: our workload is very template-heavy, so high prefix re-use is likely. But we need to understand warm vs cold starts, and also shard placement in our VPC.
[03:55] Arjun: totally. For VPC/on-prem you get additional network hop to control plane for model routing unless you run Private where control plane is customer-hosted. We observed 8-50ms extra per request on some cloud-VPC configs; on-prem can be higher if firewall inspection is in path.
[04:18] Tom: the firewall inspection is a blocker—our security team mandates TLS-inspecting proxies for egress which added jitter during previous tests.
[04:28] Maya: noted. We'll include recommended network config that avoids egress inspection for inference traffic or pins to a private peering.
[04:38] Arjun: jumping back to structured output: function/tool calling path adds a second pass when you do tool invocation flow: first pass to detect function intent, then a deterministic call, then a second pass to generate function arguments serialized as JSON. Each pass can hit KV cache differently. If you chain multiple tools the cost compounds.
[05:05] Priya: exact numbers?
[05:08] Arjun: on average a single function call flow added 12-45ms median additional latency and up to 120-200ms in p99 for small models on our infra; for larger models the absolute ms is bigger but percentage is often lower. These numbers are with batching off; with batching they can amortize but p99 still grows because of scheduling.
[05:36] Tom: you mentioned batching scheduling, can you explain the tradeoffs for our high-concurrency bursty traffic?
[05:42] Arjun: yes. Continuous batching improves throughput and reduces per-token cost, but it increases tail latency because requests wait to be batched. We support latency SLO-aware batching: you can set max wait (e.g., 5ms) and target batch size; the runtime will dispatch earlier if latency budget is nearly exhausted. For bursty workloads I'd recommend smaller max wait and aggressive autoscale to keep queues short.
[06:04] Sara: and for dedicated vs hosted, how much control do we have over those knobs?
[06:10] Maya: Dedicated gives you policy-level controls for batching windows, reserved GPUs, and pinned hosts to reduce noisy neighbour effects. Private gives the most network control but requires you to manage scaling and some infra components.
[06:25] Priya: okay, quantization: we saw problems with hallucinated JSON keys when using extreme quant modes. Which quant profiles are safe for strict schema?
[06:36] Arjun: good question. Our guidance: for strict JSON outputs stay at int8 quant or tuned 4-bit with per-channel calibration and bias correction. The aggressive 3-bit/ultra low-bit profiles can produce tokenization edge cases that break validators. We also suggest adding schema-aware sampling constraints to reduce those errors.
[06:58] Tom: does Redwood provide automatic re-calibration or should we run locally?
[07:03] Arjun: we provide recommended profiles and an auto-tune helper. For Private/on-prem we can include the calibration tool in the deploy package so you can run it against your corpus.
[07:14] Priya: nice. Can you explain where KV cache serialization sits in the stack during function calling? we saw some cache thrash in earlier tests.
[07:26] Arjun: KV cache is sharded per model-instance; when you do a function call and then request a second pass the runtime can reuse the KV across passes if the same model instance handles both. But with aggressive autoscale or non-sided routing you might hit a cold instance. The cache sharding and shard affinity are key: pinned routing for adapter-heavy workloads helps.
[07:51] Priya: so affinity reduces cold miss rate but may reduce overall pool utilization.
[07:56] Arjun: exactly. It's a utilization vs latency tradeoff.
[08:03] Sarah (sic) [note: transcript spelled Sara as Sarah in one place]: we need to quantify the CPU vs GPU split so our infra team can size hosts, any example runbooks?
[08:12] Arjun: yes, I'll attach a CPU/GPU timeline chart. For JSON strictness the CPU-side validator took ~8-30ms per output depending on complexity; GPU extra kernels could be 10-60ms per token for some constrain steps. We should run a set with your real prompts to give exact capacity numbers.
[08:36] Tom: for on-prem we might want to avoid any SDK-level validation; can runtime-only enforcement work?
[08:41] Arjun: runtime-only enforcement is supported and reduces host round trips, but it increases GPU cycles as I said. If you have spare GPU headroom that's fine; if not you can do light-weight runtime enforcement plus a fast host sanity check.
[08:58] Priya: about instrumentation: can we get token-level breakdown per-request (GPU kernels, KV hits, validation time) in the logs?
[09:06] Maya: yes, Redwood Console exposes per-token cost and latency breakdowns per request for Hosted/Dedicated and for Private we provide the same telemetry pipeline with configurable retention. We can redact sensitive data as needed.
[09:20] Tom: does the telemetry add latency to the request path?
[09:24] Arjun: telemetry is async; minimal impact. If you run offline tracing we might add minimal perturbation.
[09:33] Priya: one of our concerns is function-call chaining: we call a model to generate args for a tool, call tool, then another model call to summarize. Does KV cache persist across those tool boundaries?
[09:48] Arjun: yes if the same model instance handles them. If you call different model variants or there's an autoscale reshuffle you'll see misses. Our recommended pattern: keep hot chains on dedicated pools or pin model versions to reduce reshuffle.
[10:02] Priya: and for cost accounting when using these chains how do we attribute tokens?
[10:09] Maya: Console shows token-level attribution per route/model; for chained flows you can tag requests to get per-step cost. We also support function-level tagging in the request metadata.
[10:22] Tom: can we instrument custom tags from our side and have Redwood show per-tag metrics?
[10:27] Maya: yes, custom tags supported.
[10:30] Arjun: quick note on scheduling: we ran a batching sweep where we increased max_wait from 2ms to 20ms -- p50 improved by 18% cost-wise but p99 degraded significantly. For strict SLOs keep max_wait low.
[10:45] Priya: what about multi-tenant pools and noisy neighbour?
[10:49] Arjun: Dedicated avoids that. For hosted we use soft isolation and priority queues; cross-tenant tail can still occur but it's rare with small bursty traffic.
[10:59] Sara: are we able to run a pilot on Redwood Dedicated to validate our latency envelope before moving to Private?
[11:05] Maya: yes that's a common path. We'll provision a small dedicated pool and run your workload for a pilot period.
[11:12] Arjun: I'll outline the pilot: 1) supply prompt set and token dist, 2) Redwood runs constrained-decode microbench across quant profiles and batching configs, 3) share CSVs and a short runbook, 4) optionally run the pilot in your VPC via Private preview.
[11:32] Priya: do you have example CSVs we can see?
[11:35] Arjun: yes attaching sample CSV: columns: prompt_id, tokens_in, tokens_out, kv_hit, batch_size, gpu_ms, cpu_ms, total_ms, p50, p95, p99. The p99 numbers are the ones you should watch for.
[11:51] Tom: can you include the network hop delta when hosted seen from our VPC?
[11:55] Arjun: we can measure egress/ingress delta during the pilot, but typical cloud VPC peering adds 5-25ms; proxies/firewalls add jitter.
[12:05] Priya: anything else in terms of hard blockers?
[12:08] Arjun: security-wise we covered SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS for Private. For on-prem we recommend bringing your KMS/HSM or using our customer-managed key integration. There may be some regulatory paperwork.
[12:24] Sara: cost model: if constrained decoding increases GPU cycles, how should we budget?
[12:29] Maya: you'll get per-token and per-request cost breakdowns. For budgeting run the microbench with your corpus and multiply the per-call cost by expected monthly QPS. We can help estimate.
[12:40] Priya: a nit: we sometimes get malformed json when the model tokenizes mid-key, any tips?
[12:47] Arjun: best practice: use single-token-safe keys when possible, and pad keys with delimiters; also use a deterministic serializer and enforce a small post-process validator as insurance. The runtime's schema-aware sampling reduces those cases but not eliminates them.
[13:05] Tom: about serialization in function-calling: is the JSON created via sample decoding or via a deterministic arg-generator?
[13:12] Arjun: it's sampled but constrained; we do beam-like resampling to satisfy grammar in many cases. Deterministic generation is possible but hurts diversity and can increase latency.
[13:29] Priya: what's the recommendation for multi-tool pipelines that require strict typed arguments?
[13:34] Arjun: use a two-pass: intent detection (fast) then synchronous deterministic arg gen with strict validators; pin both passes to same instance/pool to reuse KV and reduce cold misses.
[13:46] Maya: we should talk about the configuration files for the pilot - I'll send a sample.
[13:51] Arjun: one more note on quant: bias-corrected per-layer quant helps preserve grammar tokens which are often the small set that break JSON. Also introspect logits for grammar tokens during calibration.
[14:08] Priya: good. Can you share the exact commands to run the benchmarking harness?
[14:12] Arjun: yes I'll add a README with docker run that runs 1k prompt corpus across configs (flags: --json-mode, --constrained, --quant=int8,int4 --batch-sweep=1,2,4,8 --max-wait-ms=2,5,10,20).
[14:29] Tom: can we run that harness inside our VPC to measure network impact?
[14:34] Arjun: absolutely. For Private we'll provide the same harness and you can run it locally.
[14:41] Maya: let's recap next steps.
[14:45] Maya: Redwood: Arjun will deliver the benchmark scripts and sample CSVs; Maya will send SOC2 and private deploy runbook. AtlasIQ: Tom provides prompt set and token distribution. We'll aim for a pilot in mid-December.
[15:00] Priya: that works. Anything else?
[15:05] Sara: no, thanks. Also include guidance on avoiding TLS inspection for inference egress or best-practice peering.
[15:13] Maya: will do. Thanks everyone. Meeting ends.
